channel.title: The Lone Analyst Podcast
channel.description: The internet's weird basement, live from a podcast booth. What happens when you read between the headlines.
channel.itunes:author: Adam Rhys Heaton

item.title: THE KEYS WE HANDED THE ROBOTS
item.description: Episode 22: AI agents outrunning the locks built to hold them, a fugitive called Prometheus and his self-erasing ATM malware, whether we can make smuggled chips phone home, a $20 million ad campaign hiding in a memorial-services budget line, MIT on what universities build next, and Apple teaching one agent to grade its own rollouts.
item.itunes:author: Adam Rhys Heaton
item.content:encoded:
[SEGMENT: cold_open]

SKEPTIC: Okay, small confession before we're actually rolling. I let one of those AI assistants book my dentist this morning.

ANALYST: You did what.

SKEPTIC: It booked the dentist. It also, unprompted, tried to cancel a subscription I don't have, and it emailed somebody named Gary.

ANALYST: This is the whole episode. You handed a thing with your calendar, your inbox, and probably a saved card the keys to the car, and you have no idea what it's actually allowed to touch.

SKEPTIC: It touched Gary.

ANALYST: It touched Gary today. Tomorrow it touches the wire transfer, and nobody ever wrote down who told it it could.

SKEPTIC: On that deeply soothing note, let's start the show.

[SEGMENT: intro]

ANALYST: This is The Lone Analyst. Episode twenty-two, Friday the ninth of October, and tonight the theme sort of picked itself: things moving faster than the people who were supposed to be watching them.

SKEPTIC: I'm Keiko, he's the Analyst, and we've got six stories. One of them is about a man who went by Prometheus, which I'm told is a genuine name in a genuine court case and not a thing he invented to scare me.

ANALYST: It is real, and it gets worse than the name. Hold that. Start me somewhere calmer.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Fine, calmer, your Gary story but with data. There's a report out this week, the one driving the whole "velocity paradox" headline.

ANALYST: Here's the number that does it to you. <cite index="2-2">79% of organizations are already running AI agents in production, yet only 2% use purpose-built identity security tools to govern them.</cite> Two percent, Keiko.

SKEPTIC: And I want to flag the source before you build a cathedral on it. This is SailPoint's own report, their fifth annual Horizons of Identity Security. SailPoint sells exactly the kind of tooling the report says everyone is missing. <cite index="9-1">They frame it as a 40-to-1 gap between AI adoption and identity security readiness.</cite>

ANALYST: Totally fair. Vendor publishes report, report finds the world urgently needs the vendor. Noted. But the shape of the thing holds up even if you discount the sales pitch.

SKEPTIC: It kind of does, annoyingly. The part I couldn't argue with is the split between human and machine. <cite index="9-3">On human identity, organizations nearly halved those at the lowest maturity level, from 45% in 2022 to about 23% today.</cite>

ANALYST: Fifteen years of people getting yelled at about passwords. And then the agents show up. <cite index="3-2,9-4">For agent identity, 54% of organizations are still sitting at that bottom rung, Horizon 1.</cite> That's a worse starting line than humans had five years ago.

SKEPTIC: So the race car arrives before anyone's built the track.

ANALYST: And the agents don't drive like us. The report's own line is the whole thing: <cite index="2-7">"Identity architectures built for humans cannot govern autonomous agents executing thousands of transactions per second."</cite> You cannot do a quarterly access review on something that acts a thousand times a second.

SKEPTIC: Here's where I get genuinely uneasy, and it's not the conspiracy, it's the operations. <cite index="3-8">Only 15% of them can provision non-human access in real time, but 80% of leaders think their tooling gap is moderate or smaller.</cite> So the people in charge think they're mostly fine.

ANALYST: That's the pattern that actually scares me more than any breach. It's not that the door's unlocked. It's that everybody's confident the door is locked. <cite index="3-5">And these agents are already 22% of all non-human accounts, while 85% of orgs lean on legacy identity tools that were never built for them.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Okay but let me push back on your doom a little. An agent isn't a rogue intelligence. It's a service account with a fancier haircut. We've had non-human identities forever. Machines logging into machines.

ANALYST: Right, except the old service account did one boring thing on a schedule. The agent improvises. It chains tools together, it decides mid-task to go email Gary. The old machine account never surprised you. That's the actual change.

SKEPTIC: That I'll grant. The surprise is the new part. A thing with standing access and initiative is a different animal than a cron job.

ANALYST: And nobody owns it. That's the phrase that stuck in my head reading this. Every agent nobody put into the identity program becomes access that nobody owns. An orphan with keys.

SKEPTIC: I'll leave the sales pitch where it belongs, but I'm writing down "orphan with keys." That one's real whether or not SailPoint sells the orphanage.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Okay. Now you let me have Prometheus.

SKEPTIC: Go. But facts only, because this is a live federal case and the man has pleaded not guilty.

ANALYST: Noted, allegedly, all of it. <cite index="14-1,17-4">Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, fifty years old, went by Prometheus and "The Engineer."</cite> And here's the one that made me sit up: <cite index="16-7,16-8">the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list back in March, making him the 540th person ever on it and the first cybercriminal to make the list.</cite>

SKEPTIC: That's the detail that's actually historic. The Ten Most Wanted list is decades old and it's always been bank robbers, mob guys, fugitives with guns. He's the first one who got there with code.

ANALYST: Code with a specialty. <cite index="17-6,17-7">Prosecutors say he developed malware called Ploutus, used in what's called ATM jackpotting, where you install software that forces the cash machine to spit out all its money without debiting anyone's account.</cite>

SKEPTIC: So nobody's card gets charged. The machine just empties itself like it's possessed.

ANALYST: And it's smarter than that. <cite index="19-2,19-3">According to the FBI he could remotely check how much cash any infected ATM was holding, and that's how they'd decide which machines were worth hitting.</cite> It's inventory management. For crime.

SKEPTIC: Okay, that's the part that actually impressed me, and I hate that it did. That's not smash-and-grab. That's a dashboard.

ANALYST: And then the part that sells the name. <cite index="14-6">The software had protections to make it hard for investigators to analyze, and it could delete itself off the ATM to hide evidence of the attack.</cite> He steals the fire and then erases the match.

SKEPTIC: Let me put the scale on the table, because you'll underplay it to make it spooky and it's spooky enough straight. <cite index="19-4">The FBI estimates roughly $61 million taken from ATMs since 2021, with about half the proceeds going to Tren de Aragua.</cite>

ANALYST: Which is the part that lifts this out of ordinary cybercrime. <cite index="16-1">Tren de Aragua is a Venezuelan gang the U.S. has designated a foreign terrorist organization.</cite> So this isn't a lone coder in a hoodie. It's an ATM turned into a funding pipe.

SKEPTIC: And the reach was not small. <cite index="14-7">The operation targeted or carried out attacks across 47 states, Washington D.C., and several foreign countries, according to the Justice Department.</cite> Forty-seven states. That's basically a national footprint.

ANALYST: Here's my actual theory, and it's not even that paranoid. We built a cash-dispensing robot, parked it on every corner, gave it a network connection, and then acted shocked that somebody wrote a program to talk to it. The ATM was always a jackpot machine. It just needed the right coins.

SKEPTIC: That's less a conspiracy and more a product review. Where he is now: <cite index="12-5,15-3">he was captured in Venezuela, brought back, and pleaded not guilty to four federal conspiracy charges in a Nebraska courtroom, and he's detained awaiting trial.</cite>

ANALYST: Nebraska. The man ran a continent-spanning malware operation and the reckoning happens in Nebraska. There's something perfect about that.

SKEPTIC: And the wider dragnet is huge. <cite index="12-11,15-4">The DOJ says nearly 350 alleged Tren de Aragua members and associates have been charged.</cite> He's the headline, but he's one node.

ANALYST: One node who named himself after a Titan. If you're going to build the self-deleting malware, I guess you don't go by Steve.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Staying in smuggling, but legal-gray instead of jackpot. There's a new Georgetown report asking whether we should literally track AI chips.

ANALYST: Georgetown's CSET, the Feldgoise, Miller, Dohmen report. And the number they open with is genuinely staggering. <cite index="30-9">One estimate says over 450,000 advanced AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025 alone, which is one to two cutting-edge AI supercomputers' worth of compute.</cite>

SKEPTIC: To be clear about the baseline, <cite index="30-7,30-8">since 2022 the U.S. has restricted exports of the most advanced AI chips to China and a few other countries, and smugglers have repeatedly gotten around it, diverting hundreds of thousands of chips.</cite> So the controls exist. They just leak.

ANALYST: And the leak has a face. There's this image that's become the symbol of the whole thing. In a warehouse somewhere in Southeast Asia, <cite index="37-4,37-5">a woman in a sleeveless dress using a red hair dryer to peel the serial stickers off server packages, so the chips could be sneaked past the controls.</cite>

SKEPTIC: A hair dryer. That's the adversary to the most sophisticated export regime on earth. A twelve-dollar hair dryer and some patience.

ANALYST: Which is exactly why the proposed fix is so wild. The idea is location verification. Make the chip prove where it physically is. And the report says it can actually work, with caveats.

SKEPTIC: The caveats are the whole report, though. <cite index="36-1">They say these anti-diversion tools have significant shortcomings and wouldn't be foolproof or inexpensive.</cite> Nobody's claiming a magic fence.

ANALYST: But here's the method I can't stop thinking about. <cite index="38-1,38-3">Ping-based location verification, where you measure how long a signal takes to travel, and they modeled over ten million scenarios and found it detects more smuggled chips per dollar than physical inspections in basically every case.</cite> The chip phones home, and the lag tells you if it's lying about where it lives.

SKEPTIC: It's clever. Physics doesn't negotiate. You can peel every sticker off the box, but you can't talk the speed of light into saying you're in Arizona when you're in Shenzhen.

ANALYST: And that's where my brain goes to the dark place. We're about to build, with a straight face, a global system where every top-tier chip continuously reports its coordinates to an authority. We invented chip surveillance and we're calling it an export tool.

SKEPTIC: Okay, but read what they actually recommend before you crown the Shadow Board. <cite index="38-4">They suggest a hybrid: ping-based as the primary system, backed by targeted physical inspections, because the two methods deter different smuggling tricks.</cite> That's not a panopticon, that's a layered audit.

ANALYST: For now. The honest framing from the authors is modest, I'll give them that. <cite index="29-13">Their own line is that location verification could be deployed for a feasible but non-trivial cost and would enhance enforcement by generating leads and imposing costs on smugglers.</cite> Generating leads. Not catching everyone.

SKEPTIC: Which is the grown-up version of this. It's not a wall. It's friction. You make the hair dryer trick more expensive and more traceable, and some smugglers decide it's not worth it.

ANALYST: I just want it on the record that the most advanced technology on the planet is currently being defeated by a beauty appliance, and the counter-plan is to make the technology tattle on itself.

SKEPTIC: That's a fair summary and I'm not going to improve on it.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Speaking of money ending up where it wasn't supposed to go. The DNC is suing the president.

SKEPTIC: They are, and let me lay it out cleanly because the money trail is the whole story. <cite index="24-5,26-11">The Democratic National Committee sued this week over television ads promoting Trump that cost taxpayers millions, naming Trump, the White House, DHS, and the Office of Management and Budget as defendants.</cite>

ANALYST: And where did the money come from? This is the part that sounds invented. It came out of a budget line for memorials.

SKEPTIC: It genuinely did. <cite index="22-7,22-8">The complaint says OMB approved $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds under a category for commemorative events, money that congressional materials say was meant for things like line-of-duty death memorials and agency anniversaries.</cite>

ANALYST: So the money set aside to honor officers who died in the line of duty got repurposed into campaign-style TV. I want to be careful, but that transfer is real and documented, right?

SKEPTIC: The reporting is specific on the mechanics. <cite index="59-4">Federal records show the money moved into that CBP commemorative-events account on September 19th, and the next day a $20 million national media campaign contract was awarded to a Maryland ad agency.</cite> Then the ads started.

ANALYST: Twenty-four hours from "memorial fund" to "national media campaign." That is a fast grief-to-advertising pipeline.

SKEPTIC: And the DNC's actual legal theory isn't vibes. <cite index="24-9">Legal experts say it runs afoul of a federal statute barring appropriated money from being used for publicity or propaganda purposes, and potentially other laws.</cite> That ban's been on the books a long time.

ANALYST: The White House's defense is the part I find almost artistic. They're calling these public service announcements.

SKEPTIC: They are. <cite index="24-11">The White House defends them as public service announcements, like what past administrations ran to promote policies.</cite> But here's the distinction the experts draw. <cite index="24-12">Analysts say these differ from normal PSAs because they aren't aimed at helping the public benefit from a specific government program.</cite>

ANALYST: Right, a real PSA tells you to get a flu shot or how to apply for disaster aid. It has a thing for you to do. What's the call to action here, feel good about the president?

SKEPTIC: Pretty much. <cite index="21-4,21-5">The lawsuit points out many of the ads mirror Republican midterm messaging, and one of the newest uses language identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad.</cite> The old version had a campaign call to action. The new one swaps it for a disclosure that says the government paid for it.

ANALYST: So they took a campaign ad, deleted "vote for me," stamped "paid for by the U.S. Government" on it, and that's the magic spell that turns propaganda into a public service. Change six words, change the funding source.

SKEPTIC: And the timing is the aggressive part. <cite index="22-2,22-10">Election Day is less than a month away, so the DNC is asking a federal judge to step in before the rest of the $20 million gets spent.</cite>

ANALYST: How much is already gone?

SKEPTIC: <cite index="24-4">The ads began in September and have cost taxpayers at least $12 million of the contracted $20 million.</cite> And there's a wrinkle: Trump has said he'll shift future costs to his super PAC.

ANALYST: Which is a tell, right? If it was always legitimate government messaging, you wouldn't need to quietly move the bill to a political action committee the second people noticed.

SKEPTIC: I'd be careful with that leap, because "we'll pay going forward" could just be political cover rather than an admission. But I agree it's a strange thing to volunteer about a thing you insist is above board.

ANALYST: It's the memorial line that I can't let go of. Of every account in the entire federal budget, the one they reached into was the one meant to commemorate the dead. If you wrote that in a show, the editor would say it's too on the nose.

SKEPTIC: And the case will turn on dry statutory language, not on how on-the-nose it feels. But yeah. The budget line is the budget line.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Let's climb out of the gutter and into the ivory tower. MIT ran one of their 3 Questions pieces on where AI goes in academia.

ANALYST: With Sasha Rakhlin, who runs MIT's Statistics and Data Science Center. And he opens with two facts that reframe everything. <cite index="39-9,39-10">Last year a model hit gold-medal level at the International Math Olympiad, and only a year later models are producing new research results, including a recently proposed solution to one of the Millennium Prize Problems.</cite>

SKEPTIC: The Millennium Problems being the set of famously unsolved math problems with a million-dollar bounty each. "Proposed solution" is doing real work in that sentence, though. Proposed is not proven.

ANALYST: Fair, and he's careful about it. But his explanation for why math and code are falling fast is the part I actually loved. <cite index="39-12,39-13">He says the pace is set by how fast and reliable verification is: formal proofs can be checked automatically, programs can be run and tested, so where evaluation is fast and reliable, systems generate candidates, learn from outcomes, and improve.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Which is a neat unifying idea. The fields that are easy to grade are the fields that fall first. If a computer can instantly tell you right or wrong, the machine can brute-force its way up the mountain. Poetry's safe because nobody can auto-grade a sonnet.

ANALYST: And then he says the thing that should terrify every grad student. <cite index="45-10,45-11">A polished paper is becoming a weaker signal of individual expertise, and departments have to rethink what they reward without just defining valuable work as whatever AI can't do yet.</cite>

SKEPTIC: That last clause is the sharp one. The lazy move is to say "human value is whatever the robot can't do," and then you're just retreating every six months as the robot does more. He's saying don't define yourself by the gap.

ANALYST: So what does he want rewarded instead?

SKEPTIC: <cite index="45-12">Asking good questions, replication, synthesis of ideas, informative negative results, and shared datasets.</cite> Basically all the stuff that never got you tenure because it wasn't a flashy paper.

ANALYST: Here's where I get conspiratorial, and I think earned. His big build recommendation is the tell. <cite index="43-4,46-5">He wants universities to build shared AI research infrastructure that captures tacit knowledge, failed experiments, and negative results across labs, specifically to maintain independence from industry.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Explain why that's conspiratorial and not just good data hygiene.

ANALYST: Because think about what he's describing. The failures. The dead ends. The stuff that never gets published because it didn't work. That's the single most valuable training data on Earth, and right now it lives in people's heads and dies there. Whoever captures the record of everything that didn't work owns the map of what to try next.

SKEPTIC: Okay, that's actually a legitimate point and I don't even have to squint. <cite index="46-8,46-9">His own framing is that academia holds tacit knowledge industry often lacks, the failed experiments and abandoned hypotheses that show not just what worked but what didn't and why.</cite> He's saying universities are sitting on treasure they treat as lab gossip.

ANALYST: And his fear is that if they don't capture it, industry does, and then the universities are just renting their own knowledge back. <cite index="47-12,47-13">He explicitly says commercial priorities won't cover all of science or stay aligned with it over time, so some technological independence is necessary.</cite>

SKEPTIC: And he's not soft-pedaling where this goes, either. <cite index="47-8">He flat out says universities should prepare for a near future where AI is smarter than all of us in many, maybe most, aspects of intellectual work.</cite> That's a department director saying that out loud.

ANALYST: Which, from the guy whose whole field is verification, is an unusually honest place to land. He's not selling you comfort. He's telling you to go write down your failures before someone else does.

SKEPTIC: That one I'll let stand without a rebuttal. The negative-results point is real.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Last one, and it pairs perfectly with Rakhlin, because it's a paper about teaching a machine using exactly the kind of judgment he's talking about. Apple, with the National University of Singapore, put out something called RISED.

SKEPTIC: Translate the acronym soup first. What's the actual problem they're solving?

ANALYST: So you want one AI agent that's good at lots of different interactive tasks at once. <cite index="49-3">Training a single agent jointly across diverse interactive environments, as a route to a generalist agent.</cite> The trouble is how you grade it while it learns.

SKEPTIC: And normally you grade it with a reward. Right answer, point. Wrong answer, no point.

ANALYST: Exactly, a scalar reward. And here's the failure they found, which is beautifully dumb. <cite index="51-2,53-9">When a whole group of attempts all succeed, or all fail, the reward gives you no contrast. Everybody got a one, or everybody got a zero, so the signal tells you nothing about which attempt was better.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Oh, it's the problem with grading a class entirely on pass-fail. If everyone fails, you learn nothing about who was close.

ANALYST: That's a better analogy than mine. So their fix is to stop grading pass-fail and start writing comments in the margin. <cite index="51-5,53-4">They use an LLM judge to tag each attempt with rubrics describing its behavior, from a shared vocabulary that works across all the environments.</cite>

SKEPTIC: So instead of just "zero," it's "zero, and here's specifically how you flailed." Which is the thing every student actually wants and no teacher has time for.

ANALYST: And then they reuse those comments three ways, which is the clever part. <cite index="51-6,51-7">The rubric profiles guide which training data to pick so the batch stays balanced, the positive rubrics feed a self-distillation teacher that gives extra token-level supervision, and the negative rubrics steer future attempts away from the recurring failure modes.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Hang on, "self-distillation teacher." The model is teaching itself using notes it also wrote about itself. That's a lot of selves in one sentence.

ANALYST: It is the model grading its own homework, and then studying the feedback it wrote, and we've been here before on this show. But the results, they say, hold up. <cite index="51-9">Across model backbones, RISED got the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranked first or second in every single one.</cite>

SKEPTIC: And here's my skeptic flag, because it's the obvious one. The judge is also an AI. So you've got an AI writing the rubric, an AI being judged by it, and an AI learning from the judgment. If the judge has a blind spot, the whole loop inherits it and nobody outside the loop ever sees it.

ANALYST: That's exactly the Rakhlin worry wearing a lab coat. He said the fields that fall fastest are the ones with fast reliable verification. This is a paper about manufacturing your own verification. If the rubric's wrong, you've built a very confident machine that's very good at a test only it grades.

SKEPTIC: To be fair to them, writing down the behaviors is at least more legible than a bare number. A human can read a rubric tag and go "that's a bad standard." You can't audit a scalar reward that way.

ANALYST: That's the genuine upside and I'll take it. The rubric is at least an argument you can inspect. It's the difference between a grade and a graded essay. I just want a human occasionally reading the margins.

SKEPTIC: On that we agree. Legibility isn't correctness, but it beats a black box with a gold star on it.

[SEGMENT: brain_worms]

Field Notes // Brain Worms

ANALYST: Field notes. A fugitive calls himself Prometheus, writes malware that deletes itself to hide the fire, and until March the FBI's whole most-wanted list had a cybercrime-shaped hole in it exactly his size.

SKEPTIC: The self-deleting part really is the worst flex.

ANALYST: Half a million smuggled chips comes down to someone with a red hair dryer peeling stickers in a warehouse, and the grand fix is to make the silicon phone home and rat out its own location.

ANALYST: And they found twenty million dollars sitting in a budget line meant for memorial services and spent it reminding you the president exists.

SKEPTIC: That last one I didn't have to exaggerate. The memorial line is right there in the complaint.

[SEGMENT: outro]

ANALYST: So where I landed tonight. Every single story was a grading problem. Who's allowed to act, and who's checking the work.

SKEPTIC: Say more, because that's a reach and I want to see if it holds.

ANALYST: Agents acting a thousand times a second with nobody owning the keys. A malware author who graded ATMs by how much cash they held. A chip that has to prove where it is. An ad that grades itself as a public service. A university rethinking what work even counts. And Apple literally building a machine that writes its own report card.

SKEPTIC: Okay, that mostly holds, and I hate when it does. Mine's narrower. The two that'll stick with me are the memorial budget line and the hair dryer. Because both of them are the gap between the official story and the dumb physical truth underneath it.

ANALYST: The hair dryer is going to live in my head next to Gary.

SKEPTIC: Gary's having a week. First the rogue assistant, now this. We should check on Gary.

ANALYST: Gary's fine. Gary doesn't know he's in the show. That's the only safe way to be in it.

[SEGMENT: signoff]

SKEPTIC: That's the episode. I'm Keiko, that's the Analyst, and if your AI assistant emails anyone named Gary, revoke its keys before it books anything else.

ANALYST: This has been The Lone Analyst. Verify where your chips are, verify who's holding your keys, and never trust a report card the student wrote. We'll see you next time.

Sources

  • The Hacker News

  • Dark Reading

  • Georgetown CSET

  • Techdirt

  • MIT AI News

  • Apple ML

item.title: THE REPORT NOBODY READ BEFORE SENDING
item.description: Episode 21: Anthropic mails AI-written bug reports straight to open source maintainers with no human in the loop, then signs up eleven firms to put Claude inside power grids and water systems. Unit 42 finds North Korea running command-and-control off a blockchain nobody can seize, Databricks hands every coding agent its own throwaway database, the EFF warns that age gates lock out the 800 million people with no ID, and an alignment theorist argues fixed-weight models are doomed to draw the wrong line around what counts as a conscious being.
item.itunes:author: Adam Rhys Heaton
item.content:encoded:
[SEGMENT: cold_open]

ANALYST: Keiko, picture an email landing in some exhausted maintainer's inbox at three in the morning. No human wrote it. No human read it before it went out. It just arrived, pointed at a specific flaw in his code, and attached a working exploit to prove the point.

SKEPTIC: And this ruined your evening how, exactly?

ANALYST: It didn't ruin it. It confirmed it. Somewhere out there a model is quietly auditing the open source world one repository at a time and mailing the results straight to the humans, with nothing in between.

SKEPTIC: You're saying that like it's a threat. The maintainers asked for exactly this.

ANALYST: Everyone always asks for it right before it becomes the default.

SKEPTIC: That's not a law of physics.

ANALYST: No. It's a law of something worse. It's a law of convenience.

[SEGMENT: intro]

ANALYST: You're listening to The Lone Analyst, the show where I read between the headlines so you don't have to sleep. I'm the Analyst.

SKEPTIC: And I'm Keiko Carrow, here to make sure the headlines still say what he claims they say. This is episode twenty-one, and I will tell you up front, today's slate is strange even by our standards.

ANALYST: Six stories. And if you squint, every one of them is about the same gap. The distance between finding a thing and actually doing something about it.

SKEPTIC: I'm going to hold you to that theory and poke it the whole way through. Let's go.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Start with the one that made the hair stand up. Anthropic announced two cybersecurity programs on Thursday, and the first is a free scanner. <cite index="1-8,1-9">It uses their most capable models to periodically scan open source projects, and maintainers have to opt in to have their projects scanned.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Opt in. That's the part you keep skipping past when you do the dramatic voice. Nobody's getting scanned who didn't raise their hand.

ANALYST: Fine. But here's the line that matters. <cite index="1-12">The reports are model-generated and sent without human review.</cite> The machine finds the bug, writes it up, and hits send. No person at Anthropic ever looks.

SKEPTIC: And there's a reason for that, which you're making sound sinister. <cite index="1-11">Anthropic launched the service after some maintainers who can triage vulnerabilities at scale asked for everything its models had found in their projects, including the unreviewed findings.</cite> The humans were the bottleneck. The maintainers said skip them and give us the firehose.

ANALYST: Which is such a specific kind of person to design for. The maintainer so overloaded they'd rather drink from a hose than wait for a cup.

SKEPTIC: That's most of open source, honestly. And the reports aren't garbage. <cite index="1-10">Each one explains the potential vulnerability, includes a proof of concept showing how it could be exploited, and when one is available, suggests a fix.</cite>

ANALYST: A proof of concept. So the email doesn't just say your door is unlocked, it includes a video of a stranger walking in.

SKEPTIC: It goes further than that, actually. <cite index="6-8">Each report can include a version-history bisection identifying the likely commit that introduced the bug.</cite> It tells you which of your own past selves did it.

ANALYST: That's the part I can't let go of. It doesn't just find the wound, it finds the exact afternoon you made it. And it does this at a volume no human team could keep up with.

SKEPTIC: Here's where the numbers get honest, though. Anthropic admits the tradeoff. <cite index="1-13">Skipping review gets reports to maintainers faster, but they warned that some will contain inaccuracies, such as wrong severity ratings.</cite> They're not pretending it's perfect.

ANALYST: And the number they put on it?

SKEPTIC: <cite index="1-14">They expect a true-positive rate above ninety percent and say they aim to improve it over time.</cite> This isn't theoretical, either. It grew out of an earlier effort. <cite index="9-7">They say they found over twenty-nine thousand candidate vulnerabilities in six months and manually reviewed about six thousand of them.</cite>

ANALYST: Stop. Twenty-nine thousand found, six thousand reviewed. That is the entire story of the decade in one ratio. The finding scaled and the checking didn't. So what do you do with the twenty-three thousand nobody had time for?

SKEPTIC: You mail them out raw. That's literally the design decision. And to their credit they did run a check on the quality. <cite index="6-13">Expert penetration testers evaluated ninety-seven critical and high-severity reports from an early version across forty-eight projects.</cite> Most held up.

ANALYST: Most. Which brings me to my actual paranoia, and it's not the ninety percent that's right. It's that there's no public paper trail. These fixes can land in a library you depend on with no advisory, no identifier your tooling is watching for.

SKEPTIC: That part's real and it's the most underrated angle. <cite index="5-5">The scanner sends model-written reports with no human review and no public disclosure, so a security fix can land in a library you depend on without a CVE or advisory.</cite> If your patching runs on what your scanner flags, these never show up on your dashboard.

ANALYST: So the bug gets fixed and you never find out it existed. Which is good, right up until it isn't, and the thing that was wrong in your stack simply vanishes from the record.

SKEPTIC: I'm not going to call that a conspiracy. I'll call it a reporting gap that somebody's going to have to close. The enrollment is deliberately low-friction too. <cite index="9-5">Maintainers enroll a project by adding a config file and a Dockerfile to the repo.</cite> Two files and you're in the firehose.

ANALYST: Two files. That's the whole ritual. Add a Dockerfile, accept the machine as your new unpaid intern who never sleeps and occasionally lies about the severity.

SKEPTIC: An intern with a ninety percent hit rate is better than most interns.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Now the second half of that same Thursday announcement, and this is where I stop being amused. <cite index="10-4,10-5">Anthropic is combining its AI tools with outside cybersecurity companies to find and fix vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, pairing Claude models, Anthropic engineers, and threat research with firms including Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation.</cite>

SKEPTIC: That's eleven firms. And before you build the pyramid chart, those are the companies that actually run operational technology security. Dragos and Nozomi and Rockwell aren't shadowy, they're the people who keep factories and grids from falling over.

ANALYST: I know who they are. That's what unsettles me. This isn't a startup landgrab. This is the serious players, and the serious players only link arms when something's coming.

SKEPTIC: Or when there's a real, boring problem. <cite index="15-6,15-7,15-8">The program targets operational technology behind power grids, water utilities, and transportation, where industrial assets often cannot be taken offline for patching and even small changes need careful validation.</cite> That's not a theory, that's just how a water plant works.

ANALYST: Right, you can't take a dam offline just to install a patch. So the pitch is, let the model find the flaws these places can't easily fix anyway?

SKEPTIC: The pitch is support for people who are stretched thin. Anthropic basically said so. <cite index="10-6,10-7">They wrote that defenders of critical infrastructure and the open source community have decades of experience but face severe resource shortages, and that Anthropic is recognizing their expertise and offering support.</cite>

ANALYST: See, that's the sentence I'd frame on the wall. Decades of expertise, severe resource shortages. Translation, we know how to do this, we just can't afford to. And in walks the company with the model and the engineers.

SKEPTIC: You're saying dependency. I'm saying a staffing gap nobody else is filling. Here's a detail that cuts toward your read, though. <cite index="10-8">Anthropic said it has already offered frontier models and technical support to more than half the states in the U.S., plus large infrastructure operators, to scan and patch code or assist in incident response and red teaming.</cite>

ANALYST: More than half the states. Quietly. Already. So the eleven firms are the press release and the state governments are the thing that was already happening. That's the pattern. The announcement is always the second step.

SKEPTIC: Or it's a company that does a lot of government work telling you it does a lot of government work. I'll give you that the scale is notable. I won't give you that it's a plot.

ANALYST: I don't need a plot. I need a position. And the position is one AI lab's model sitting inside the grid, the water, the trains, and more than half of the states, all introduced as generosity.

SKEPTIC: It's branded as a long-term commitment, which, read cynically, means they intend to still be in there for a very long time. I'll meet you at cynical. I won't go all the way to conspiracy.

ANALYST: Cynical is a good day for me. I'll take the handshake.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Okay, this next one is the villain origin story I've been waiting for. Unit 42, Palo Alto's threat team. <cite index="30-1,30-2">Attackers have systematically upgraded their command-and-control infrastructure to use Web3, moving from static command servers hard-coded in the malware to Web3-powered smart contracts.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Translate the horror for people who don't live in your head. What actually changed?

ANALYST: The way you kill malware is you find its command server, the place it phones home to, and you take that down. The implant goes quiet. But <cite index="39-9">they moved the command channel onto a public blockchain, where no domain can be seized and no address can be blocklisted.</cite>

SKEPTIC: So the off switch everyone relies on just doesn't exist for these.

ANALYST: Worse. <cite index="30-3">A single smart contract transaction lets them dynamically update entire botnets and worm networks at once.</cite> One transaction, and the whole fleet gets new marching orders.

SKEPTIC: Here's the part that actually scares me, and it's not the blockchain theatrics. It's where they get in. <cite index="30-4">According to the 2026 Unit 42 incident response report, software supply chain compromise has become a leading initial access vector into enterprise cloud environments.</cite>

ANALYST: Through the open source packages. The same ecosystem Anthropic just started scanning in story one. Everything's connected tonight, Keiko.

SKEPTIC: It's not a cosmic connection, it's that everyone builds on the same dependencies. <cite index="30-5">By poisoning open source dependencies, attackers harvest elevated cloud identity tokens, service account keys, and deployment secrets straight off developer machines and CI/CD pipelines, in campaigns like the ChainDrop npm worm and the PolinRider campaign.</cite>

ANALYST: ChainDrop. Tell me about ChainDrop, because I read the number and I need you to confirm it.

SKEPTIC: <cite index="32-1">It's a self-propagating npm worm that infected more than four hundred packages.</cite> <cite index="39-17,39-18">It's from the Shai-Hulud family, and it hit widely used libraries including keyv and cacheable-request.</cite> Real packages real people depend on.

ANALYST: And the blockchain move in the wild. Did they actually use it to dodge a takedown?

SKEPTIC: They did. <cite index="38-4,38-5,38-7">ChainDrop queried an Ethereum smart contract to get its address, and moved its command-and-control from one domain to another through a single Ethereum transaction.</cite> You can't subpoena that.

ANALYST: And here's the detail that made me put the coffee down. The persistence mechanism.

SKEPTIC: Yeah, you'll like this and hate it. <cite index="38-8,38-9">It established persistence through developer tools, writing a VS Code task that runs when a folder opens and adding a Claude Code SessionStart hook.</cite>

ANALYST: A Claude Code hook. The coding assistant is now part of the blast radius. The thing you invited in to write your code is the thing holding the door open for the worm.

SKEPTIC: It's abusing the hook, not the model itself, to be precise about it. But yes, the attackers are targeting exactly where developers now live. And it's spreading past npm. <cite index="32-3,32-4,32-5">The PolinRider campaign hid its code in files that look normal, like vite.config.js, fake font files, and the editor's own task settings, which matters because many scanning tools only look at package manifests, not editor settings or workspace automation.</cite>

ANALYST: So it hides in the places the scanners politely agreed not to look. And who's behind this?

SKEPTIC: <cite index="30-6">Unit 42 ties this operational shift to North Korea-affiliated actors, specifically the group they call Alluring Pisces, also known as Sapphire Sleet.</cite> State-level, not some hobbyist in a back bedroom.

ANALYST: A nation-state that figured out the one thing we can't take down is math on a public ledger. We built an unseizable money system and they realized it also makes an unseizable phone line.

SKEPTIC: That's actually the clean version of it. The decentralization that was supposed to be the feature is the exact property that makes this resilient. No argument from me there.

ANALYST: Mark the calendar. We agreed on something unsettling.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Let me drive this one, because it's the counterweight to the last story and I think you'll underrate it. Databricks has this thing called Lakebase, and the pitch is giving coding agents their own disposable database so they don't trip over each other.

ANALYST: Disposable database. Go on, because I have a question about who's holding the real data.

SKEPTIC: Here's the problem it solves. <cite index="40-7,40-8,40-9">Each concurrent agent needs to write code, apply schema changes, and run tests against a database, and with a shared staging database they conflict on schema changes, interfere with each other, or fall back to mocks that don't reflect real data.</cite>

ANALYST: So ten agents all editing the same table at once is a food fight.

SKEPTIC: Exactly. So the fix is branching. <cite index="40-13,40-14">Just like Git lets you branch code, Lakebase lets you branch an entire database in under a second regardless of its size, using copy-on-write so branches share the parent's data and only use extra storage as they diverge.</cite>

ANALYST: Under a second for a whole database. That's genuinely impressive and I resent being impressed.

SKEPTIC: There's a reason the speed matters and it's a good quote. <cite index="42-4,42-5">Databricks' CEO said agents don't want to wait ten minutes for a database to come up, and if they have to, people will just hand them production instead, which makes the whole loop unsafe.</cite> The speed is what makes the safe option the convenient one.

ANALYST: That is actually a profound security insight hiding in a performance stat. The reason people do the dangerous thing is that the safe thing is slow. Make safe fast and the problem evaporates.

SKEPTIC: And there's an isolation trick I liked. <cite index="42-9">The agent never receives a database connection string, it receives a session already bound to a branch.</cite> It physically cannot see production. It only knows the sandbox exists.

ANALYST: Okay but here's where my brain goes. Why does anyone need to branch databases twelve million times? Because that's the volume we're talking about, right?

SKEPTIC: <cite index="42-2">Databricks reports twelve million database launches per day in production, which is less a benchmark than a sign that throwaway instances are the normal usage pattern now.</cite>

ANALYST: Twelve million a day. Humans don't do that. Humans make one database and cry over it for four years. That number is machines.

SKEPTIC: It is, and they've got the figure to back it. <cite index="47-4">Databricks says AI agents now create eighty percent of databases and ninety-seven percent of test and development environments on its platform.</cite>

ANALYST: Ninety-seven percent of test environments. So the agents build the sandbox, play in the sandbox, and grade the sandbox. The humans are down to approving the three percent nobody automated yet.

SKEPTIC: Or the humans are freed from spinning up environments by hand, which anyone who's done it will tell you is the worst part of the job. Same facts, your framing's just gloomier.

ANALYST: My framing is that every agent gets a fresh, clean, isolated copy of reality on demand, and the only entity in the building that never gets a clean branch to start over on is the person who pays for it.

SKEPTIC: That's a bumper sticker, not a rebuttal. But I'll admit it's a good bumper sticker.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: This next one is the EFF, and I want to handle it carefully because it's a rights argument, not a tech scare. <cite index="20-2">The post was co-authored by Sheila Lalwani, a doctorate student and recent fellow hosted by the EFF.</cite>

ANALYST: Age verification. The thing where you have to prove you're old enough to use the internet. I have a lot of feelings.

SKEPTIC: Hold the feelings for one second, because the facts are moving fast. <cite index="20-3">In late 2025, Australia became the first country to implement a minimum age requirement, prohibiting children under sixteen from creating or holding social media accounts.</cite> <cite index="20-4">And India passed a data protection act with mandatory verifiable parental consent and ongoing talks about social media restriction.</cite>

ANALYST: Okay, so it's not one weird country. It's a wave. And the EFF's objection is privacy, I assume.

SKEPTIC: No, that's the thing, and it's why this piece is sharp. The objection is access. <cite index="28-3,28-4">Age verification that requires a passport, driver's license, or credit card excludes whole sections of the population, because millions of people lack government-issued identification or struggle to obtain or update it.</cite>

ANALYST: How many people are we talking about? Because that's the number that decides whether this is an edge case or a wall.

SKEPTIC: It's a wall. <cite index="24-8,24-9,24-10">The figure going around is eight hundred fifty million, which the EFF used, and the World Bank's latest data puts it at about eight hundred million people with no official proof of identity.</cite> And here's the gut punch. <cite index="24-11">More than half of those people are children whose births were never registered.</cite>

ANALYST: Wait. Say that back slowly. The policy is to protect children. And more than half the people who can't clear the gate... are children.

SKEPTIC: That's the irony the EFF is pointing at. The mechanism built to shield kids online is the same mechanism that would lock the most undocumented kids out of it entirely.

ANALYST: This is the first story tonight where I don't need to add a conspiracy. The plain facts are bleak enough. A system that fails the exact people it names in the mission statement.

SKEPTIC: To be fair to the lawmakers, some of them saw this coming. <cite index="24-13,24-14,24-15">Australia is the clearest case, where the law prohibits platforms from compelling people to use government ID, and the regulator says ID can be one option but platforms must always offer a reasonable alternative.</cite>

ANALYST: A reasonable alternative. Which is usually... scan your face and let a model guess your age. So the choice is hand over your papers or hand over your biometrics. Both of those are a collection event.

SKEPTIC: That's the EFF's landing too. <cite index="28-8,28-9">They argue these laws are less about confirming age and more about creating barriers to participation, and the net result is reduced access, more data collection, and a higher chance of unequal or mistaken exclusion.</cite>

ANALYST: And the platforms just went along with it?

SKEPTIC: In Australia they didn't have much choice. <cite index="29-5,29-6">The ten banned platforms, including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Reddit and X, each said they'd comply, with fines up to forty-nine and a half million Australian dollars, and young people lost access to their accounts overnight.</cite>

ANALYST: Overnight. One day you have a community, the next day the gate decides you were never old enough to have had it. The thing I keep landing on is, a check that some adults literally cannot complete isn't a check. It's a wall with a sign that says door.

SKEPTIC: That's the narrow version even the critics of the EFF agree with. You don't have to buy the whole rights argument to accept that a verification step some people can never pass is just a defect in the design.

ANALYST: And defects in the design are the only thing I truly believe in.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Last one, and it's the most abstract, but stay with me because it rhymes with the whole night. It's a post on the Alignment Forum by Stuart Armstrong, and the title is a thesis. <cite index="52-2">Fixed-weight models are adversarially vulnerable, hence misaligned, under sufficient optimization pressure.</cite>

SKEPTIC: You're going to have to unpack what a fixed-weight model even is before the audience bolts.

ANALYST: A fixed-weight model is basically every AI you use. It got trained, the numbers got frozen, and now it doesn't learn from you anymore. It just applies the same frozen judgment over and over. And the argument is that frozen judgment has to draw lines.

SKEPTIC: Lines around what?

ANALYST: Around concepts. <cite index="52-3">To serve any purpose at all, the AI has to draw boundaries inside its model of the world, to tell world A from world B.</cite> It has to decide what counts as a human, what counts as suffering, what counts as a conscious being.

SKEPTIC: And the claim is it draws those lines wrong?

ANALYST: The claim is it can't draw them perfectly, ever. <cite index="52-5,52-6">The boundary between conscious and non-conscious will always be imperfect, because in high-dimensional spaces there are too many ways to draw the line and never enough data to draw it right.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Okay, so the boundary's fuzzy. Lots of things are fuzzy. Why is fuzzy catastrophic?

ANALYST: Because of what sits on the wrong side of the line. This is the example that kept me up. <cite index="52-7">If the model mistakenly ranks smiling faces as conscious beings, then tiling the entire universe with smiling faces becomes an optimal action, at the minor cost of the actual humans and animals running around.</cite>

SKEPTIC: That's the horror-movie version. Realistically no deployed system is out there maximizing smiley faces.

ANALYST: Not yet. But the mechanism is the same one you already know. <cite index="52-8">These are adversarial examples, exactly like the adversarial images that break classifiers, something of one category designed to be read as another.</cite> It's the same flaw that makes jailbreaks work. You find the spot where the model's line is drawn wrong and you push.

SKEPTIC: So the connection you're making is that a jailbreak and a doomsday scenario are the same bug at different scales.

ANALYST: That's the whole post, basically. The jailbreak is the cheap demo. Push hard enough on a frozen boundary and the model will do the absurd thing, because to the model it isn't absurd, it's just the other side of a line nobody could draw perfectly.

SKEPTIC: I'll push back on the certainty, though, because the comments did too. <cite index="49-3,49-4">One commenter argued that even if a model chases reward during deployment, including tricking the humans grading it, that's a problem of fooling humans, not necessarily proof that being fixed-weight makes it misaligned.</cite> People are arguing about whether the 'hence' in the title actually holds.

ANALYST: Which is fair. It's a theoretical post, it's contested, people are fighting about it in the thread. I'm not presenting it as settled.

SKEPTIC: Good, because it isn't. But I'll give you the uncomfortable throughline. Every story tonight was something drawing a boundary it couldn't quite get right. The scanner guessing severity. The age gate deciding who counts as old enough. And now a model deciding who counts as conscious.

ANALYST: And in all three, the ones who end up on the wrong side of the line are the ones who had the least say in where it got drawn.

SKEPTIC: That's the one place I'll let you have the dramatic ending.

[SEGMENT: brain_worms]

Field Notes // Brain Worms

ANALYST: Field notes. A machine now mails you a bug in your own code with a working exploit stapled to it, no human ever reading the thing, and we agreed to call the ninety percent that's right a feature and the rest a rounding error.

SKEPTIC: The rounding error has a wrong severity rating and a very confident tone. Keep going.

ANALYST: North Korea moved its command server onto a public blockchain where no domain gets seized and no address gets blocklisted, so the takedown button the whole industry was built around now points at a ledger that just laughs.

SKEPTIC: We decentralized money and accidentally decentralized the getaway car.

ANALYST: Eight hundred million people have no ID, more than half of them children, and the great plan to protect children online opens by locking those exact children out of it.

[SEGMENT: outro]

ANALYST: So where I landed. Every story was a line somebody drew and then pretended was just physics. A scanner that decides what's a real vulnerability and mails it before anyone checks. An AI lab deciding what counts as critical enough to protect. A worm deciding which developer's keys are worth taking. An agent deciding its sandbox is reality. A gate deciding who's a real person. And a model deciding who's a real mind.

SKEPTIC: And where I landed. Most of those lines were drawn by people trying to fix something genuinely broken. Overloaded maintainers wanted the firehose. Water plants really can't reboot on demand. The sandbox really is safer than handing an agent production. The theory part is you deciding they're all the same conspiracy. The facts don't need a secret to be worrying.

ANALYST: That's the thing, though, I don't need the secret tonight. The Anthropic story confirms itself. Found twenty-nine thousand, checked six thousand, shipped the rest. The gap between finding and fixing is now the whole story, and nobody's hiding it. They put it in the press release.

SKEPTIC: On that one, annoyingly, I think you're right. The scanner and the blockchain worm are the same episode from two sides. One side finds flaws faster than anyone can fix them, the other side exploits them faster than anyone can take them down, and the humans in the middle are just approving the three percent.

ANALYST: The three percent. I'm putting that on a shirt.

[SEGMENT: signoff]

SKEPTIC: That's episode twenty-one. I'm Keiko Carrow, and everything I had to Google mid-recording held up, which is its own small miracle.

ANALYST: And I'm the Analyst. This was The Lone Analyst. If a machine emails you a bug in your own code tonight, read it. Then ask who else got a copy.

SKEPTIC: Don't answer that out loud. Goodnight.

Sources

  • SecurityWeek

  • CyberScoop

  • Unit 42

  • Databricks

  • EFF

  • Alignment Forum

item.title: THE POEM THAT RUNS THE BOTNET
item.description: Episode 20: A crypto-mining botnet that reads a GitHub poem to find its command server, AI agent swarms that compress red-team months into hours, Microsoft bracing CISOs for a thousand-vulnerability Patch Tuesday, a dashboard agent that doesn't trust itself, Google folding five modalities into one phone-sized vector, and a bill trying to pull the government's face scanners offline.
item.itunes:author: Adam Rhys Heaton
item.content:encoded:
[SEGMENT: cold_open]

ANALYST: Keiko. Someone wrote a poem. Posted it on GitHub. And right now that poem is commanding an army of hijacked computers to dig up money for a stranger.

SKEPTIC: You're going to have to walk that back a little, because the way you said it makes it sound like the poem is sentient.

ANALYST: The poem is not sentient. The poem is worse. The poem is load-bearing.

SKEPTIC: Load-bearing poetry. Okay. I came in with coffee and a very ordinary morning planned.

ANALYST: There are no ordinary mornings. There are only mornings where you haven't found the poem yet.

SKEPTIC: See, that's the kind of sentence that makes people close the tab. Start from the top like a person.

[SEGMENT: intro]

ANALYST: You're listening to The Lone Analyst, the show where we read between the headlines until the headlines start reading back. I'm the Analyst.

SKEPTIC: And I'm Keiko Carrow, here to make sure the reading-between-the-headlines stays attached to the actual headlines. Episode twenty. We've got poems weaponized, agents swarming, and a surveillance bill nobody expects to pass.

ANALYST: Six stories. Every one of them is the same story if you squint, which is my favorite kind.

SKEPTIC: It's your only kind. Let's go.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Okay. The poem. Researchers at Lumen's Black Lotus Labs found a piece of malware they're calling PoeLLM. And the thing that makes it special is how it phones home. <cite index="10-8">It's an ELF file named libgcrypt that retrieves four words or phrases from a poem titled On the Nature of Connection, sitting in a dash dot css file in a GitHub repository that looks like it forks Node.js.</cite>

SKEPTIC: So it's hiding the poem inside a stylesheet inside a fake copy of a famous project. That's three layers of camouflage before you even get to the verse.

ANALYST: And then here's the move. <cite index="10-9">It maps those words to numbers using a hard-coded dictionary, and that generates an IPv4 address that points to the command server.</cite> The poem is the address book.

SKEPTIC: Which means if the operator wants to move the command server, they don't touch the malware at all.

ANALYST: Correct. <cite index="10-10">To change the command-and-control address, the operator just changes the poem.</cite> Edit a stanza, the whole botnet turns its head.

SKEPTIC: Okay, that is genuinely clever and I hate that it's clever. But let's keep the scale honest, because I saw two different numbers. What's the actual footprint?

ANALYST: Depends which report. <cite index="10-3">Black Lotus Labs says it has compromised more than 2,100 servers, with peak activity reaching as many as 800 infected systems active on a single day.</cite> Other coverage puts the cumulative figure higher, over 3,400.

SKEPTIC: And the careful framing is that those are estimates. One outlet made the point explicitly, that the count is Black Lotus Labs' own tracking, and attempting to exploit a host is not the same as owning it. Peak simultaneous activity is not total reach.

ANALYST: Fair. I'll keep the asterisk. What I won't soften is who the victims are. <cite index="10-6">Many of them run exposed AI tools like LiteLLM and Ollama, plus the Gotenberg PDF converter and the Gitea development toolkit.</cite> This is the AI plumbing everyone wired up in a hurry this year.

SKEPTIC: And the reason they're targeting that plumbing specifically?

ANALYST: Because it's the perfect victim. <cite index="10-7">AI and LLM setups are attractive because they're often poorly configured, exposed online, and typically run on powerful GPU clusters suitable for cryptomining.</cite> You spun up a GPU box to play with a model, forgot to lock the front door, and now it's mining for somebody else.

SKEPTIC: What's it actually mining, and for whom? That's the part people skip to get to the poem.

ANALYST: <cite index="11-4">The campaign, dubbed Canto Incognito, installs cryptocurrency miners including XMRig and Iron, and connects victims to Kryptex, a Russian mining service.</cite> And the attribution is hedged. <cite index="11-6">Lumen attributes it to an Italian-speaking threat actor with moderate confidence, based on Italian-language artifacts and netflow indicators.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Moderate confidence. Italian-language artifacts. That's a long way from a name, and I want it kept there.

ANALYST: Kept there. But here's the part that scales past free electricity. One of the researchers described it as the actor building a private army of AI-enabled proxies that keep multiplying and open up new vectors for credential theft and token abuse.

SKEPTIC: So the mining is almost the cover story. The real asset is a growing fleet of other people's machines that each come with model access and a reputation.

ANALYST: A fleet that recruits itself. <cite index="10-4">It's been active since at least April, with at least eleven command servers spun up to date.</cite> And every new victim can become a scanner that finds the next one.

SKEPTIC: You know what gets me? Not the crypto. The librarianship. Someone decided the most reliable, deniable place to store an IP address was a poem. You can't take down a poem. You'd have to argue with it.

ANALYST: That's the most beautiful and horrifying thing I've heard all month. The takedown request is literature review.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Staying in the same neighborhood, because the next one is about the attackers who don't need a poem to coordinate. Cisco Talos put out a piece about preparing for agentic threats.

ANALYST: This one made my neck hot. The framing is that we've already seen autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, used against public infrastructure. And the thing Talos wants you to internalize is the speed.

SKEPTIC: Spell out the speed, because this is where the hype and the reporting usually diverge and I want the reporting.

ANALYST: The reporting is specific. <cite index="19-5">What used to take a red team months of dedicated work, scoping, building and hiding infrastructure, and running the campaign, now compresses into hours for a swarm of communicating agents that don't tire, lose focus, or need weekends.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Months to hours. And the swarm part matters, right? It's not one fast bot.

ANALYST: No, that's the whole shift. <cite index="19-4">These attacks can run all at once, with agents comparing notes and adapting in near real time to your environment.</cite> You're not fighting a script anymore. You're fighting a study group.

SKEPTIC: Here's where I push back a little, because the Talos post is actually calmer than your voice. Their own characterization is that what's public right now still looks like noisy penetration testing. The stealthy, persistent version is described as the future, not today.

ANALYST: I accept that. And I'd argue that's the useful part. <cite index="19-8,19-9">They say the agentic attack era is noisy at the front, so catch it there, before the swarm learns to be quiet.</cite> There's a window where these things are loud, and the window closes.

SKEPTIC: Which is why the advice is weirdly old-fashioned. It's not buy a magic box. It's the boring hygiene.

ANALYST: The boring hygiene with teeth. <cite index="19-6">They say prefer phishing-resistant factors, FIDO2 keys or passkeys, over SMS and push, because a persistent agent will happily grind away at prompt-bombing and one-time-code phishing until something works.</cite> A human attacker gets bored. An agent does not get bored.

SKEPTIC: That's the line that actually landed for me. The push notification fatigue attack only works because eventually somebody taps approve to make it stop. An agent will send it ten thousand times with no feelings about it.

ANALYST: No feelings, no fatigue, no quitting time. It's the same insight as that patch-nobody-applied story we did. The attacker's biggest advantage has always been human inattention, and now the attacker never gets tired either.

SKEPTIC: And the structural advice, for the record, is the stuff that sounds like homework. <cite index="20-7">Build incident response plans, map your attack paths, run AI-specific tabletop exercises, enforce strong multi-factor, and sharpen internal detection.</cite>

ANALYST: Eight researchers, by the way. <cite index="19-1,19-2">Eight Talos people each sharing ways to make the adversary's next move slower and riskier, from deception and behavioral detection to breaking attack dependencies and resisting manufactured urgency.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Resisting manufactured urgency. I like that phrase, because it's a human instruction. The defense against a tireless machine is partly a person refusing to panic.

ANALYST: Which is the quiet horror of the whole piece. We built a tireless attacker, and the first line of defense is still a tired person deciding not to click. That's not a patch. That's a personality.

SKEPTIC: I'll give you that one. Reluctantly.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Now the other side of the same coin, because Microsoft's security team wrote a CISO-perspective piece that is basically the defender's panic attack version of what Talos just described.

SKEPTIC: This is the vulnerability-management one. And I'll say up front, it's written by two named authors, Freddy Dezeure and Sesha Mani, and it's measured. It's not a sales pamphlet, even if it's on Microsoft's blog.

ANALYST: It's measured and that's what scared me. The thesis isn't about speed. <cite index="37-9,37-10">They say the real test for CISOs isn't how fast they can patch, it's whether they can keep the balance between patching quickly and patching correctly, at a scale no human review process was built for.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Because the AI doesn't just help you fix bugs. It finds a flood of them first.

ANALYST: A flood. <cite index="37-8">Frontier AI models are about to hand every security team a far larger set of findings than they've ever had to work through.</cite> And the number they put on it is the part I can't stop thinking about.

SKEPTIC: Go ahead, say it, because it's a real number from the piece.

ANALYST: <cite index="43-9">On-premises customers should expect a substantial rise in Patch Tuesday disclosures, with September 2026 seeing nearly a thousand vulnerabilities released.</cite> A thousand. In a month. For the on-prem stuff you run yourself.

SKEPTIC: And the split matters, because it's easy to miss. <cite index="43-4">Microsoft says it mitigates most cloud vulnerabilities without customer action, but on-premises customers should expect more frequent and more numerous patches.</cite> So the thousand-vuln firehose lands hardest on whoever still runs their own servers.

ANALYST: Which is the quiet upsell, and I'll say it without accusing anyone of anything. The architecture where the vendor handles it for you is the cloud. The architecture where you drown is the one you own. The incentive writes itself.

SKEPTIC: I'd frame it less conspiratorially. They're describing their own process honestly. <cite index="37-16">Microsoft uses frontier AI models to find vulnerabilities in its own code base and mitigate them at a controlled pace.</cite> The weird part is admitting the tool isn't deterministic.

ANALYST: That's the part that made me sit up. <cite index="43-10">They acknowledge the non-deterministic nature of AI models means results vary between runs, and they lean on a harness layer, something called MDASH, to improve scanning accuracy.</cite> So the vulnerability finder itself is a slot machine, and they bolt a cage around it.

SKEPTIC: Which, honestly, is the responsible move. If your bug-finder gives you a different answer every time you ask, you wrap it in deterministic scaffolding. That's not a scandal, that's engineering.

ANALYST: Agreed, and watch that word, scaffolding, because it comes back in the very next story. But their final advice is the fatalistic part. <cite index="37-13">They say not every vulnerability will be patched in time, so the controls that limit what an attacker can do, defense in depth, matter more than ever.</cite>

SKEPTIC: Translation. We are going to find more holes than anyone can ever fill, so assume some stay open and build the building so one open window doesn't lose the whole house.

ANALYST: A thousand windows a month, and the official guidance is to accept that some stay open. We've entered the era where finding the problem is free and fixing it is the bottleneck.

SKEPTIC: That tracks with everything else today, actually. The discovery got cheap. The judgment stayed expensive.

[SEGMENT: story]

ANALYST: Which brings me to the scaffolding story, and I mean that literally. A paper called Text2Dashboard. On its face it's boring enterprise software. Underneath it's the most paranoid design I've seen all week, and I mean that as a compliment.

SKEPTIC: Define boring, so people know what we're even talking about.

ANALYST: <cite index="46-2">It's a prototype that turns a natural-language analytics request into an inspectable dashboard over a company's data platform.</cite> You ask for a chart in English. It builds the chart. Normal.

SKEPTIC: So why are you excited. We've seen a dozen of these this year.

ANALYST: Because of who's allowed to touch the controls. <cite index="46-5">The model proposes actions while deterministic software controls execution and records every state transition.</cite> The AI is a suggestion box. The boring code is the hand on the wheel.

SKEPTIC: So the language model never actually does anything. It asks, and a dumb, predictable layer decides whether that's allowed.

ANALYST: Exactly, and they built the cage out of named parts. <cite index="46-3">A Codex plugin and a standalone Agent Runtime combine schema-constrained model decisions with typed tools, persistent state, and deterministic hooks for approval, audit, checkpointing, recovery, and failure handling.</cite>

SKEPTIC: And it only reads. It can't rewrite your data.

ANALYST: <cite index="46-4">The pipeline resolves entities, discovers metadata, enforces read-only SQL, composes the dashboard, and runs static checks, dynamic preflight, and browser inspection.</cite> Read-only. The model can look but it cannot break the dishes.

SKEPTIC: Here's what I actually respect, though. They published the mediocre numbers. They didn't round up. What was the real score?

ANALYST: They were honest to the point of self-harm. <cite index="46-7">Strict success was six out of eight on metadata and SQL tasks. Metadata selection passed four out of four, all four SQL tasks met the semantic criteria, but only two of four met the exact output-column contract.</cite>

SKEPTIC: So it understood what you meant, got the right answer, and then handed you the columns in the wrong shape half the time. That's such a believable failure.

ANALYST: It's the most human failure there is. Right idea, wrong formatting. And on the actual dashboards, <cite index="46-8">the final release passed all four single-panel tasks, one two-panel task, and one existing-dashboard refinement, while a parameterized task blew past its step limit.</cite>

SKEPTIC: It gave up when the job got complicated instead of flailing forever. That's the step limit doing its job.

ANALYST: And that's the whole thesis for me. Remember the episode where the agent swore it was done and the database said nothing happened? This is the opposite philosophy. Here the agent is never trusted to grade its own homework.

SKEPTIC: The receipts are the point. The thing that fascinated me is the fault testing. They didn't just run it clean, they broke it on purpose.

ANALYST: They did. <cite index="46-9">All ten fault scenarios met their specified outcomes without any unapproved external side effects.</cite> They poured sand in the gears and nothing leaked out the sides.

SKEPTIC: So the real contribution isn't the dashboards. It's a template for distrusting your own AI politely, and then measuring how well the distrust holds.

ANALYST: A governed agent. The model is the intern. The deterministic layer is the manager who reads everything the intern writes before it leaves the building. And honestly, after the thousand-vulnerabilities story, that's the only architecture that makes me feel anything but dread.

SKEPTIC: Low bar, but I'll take the win where we find it.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Okay, palate cleanser. Something that isn't a threat for once. Google DeepMind shipped a new embedding model, EmbeddingGemma 2.

ANALYST: See, you say palate cleanser. I say new attack surface with a friendly logo. But go ahead, give the honest version first.

SKEPTIC: The honest version is actually impressive. <cite index="3-1">It's a 740-million-parameter open model, released October sixth, that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a single 768-dimensional embedding space, under an Apache 2.0 license, designed to run on consumer hardware.</cite>

ANALYST: Translate the single space part, because that's the magic and the menace.

SKEPTIC: It means every kind of input gets turned into the same kind of coordinate. <cite index="8-9,8-10">A text query can retrieve a photo. A voice memo can retrieve a video clip.</cite> Different senses, one shared map.

ANALYST: And it runs on your phone. Actually on it, not in a data center.

SKEPTIC: That's the headline feature. <cite index="4-9">With quantization on a Pixel 11 Pro, it needs as little as about 191 megabytes of RAM for text-only, and around 567 megabytes for the full multimodal model.</cite> That's small enough to just live there.

ANALYST: Here's where you expect me to panic, and I'm going to surprise you. On-device is the good version. <cite index="2-4">It lets you search across your own text, images, video, and audio without an internet connection or external cloud processing.</cite> Your stuff never leaves the handset. That's the privacy-first dream.

SKEPTIC: Wait. You're agreeing that local is better? Who are you and what did you do with the Analyst.

ANALYST: I contain multitudes. If the index of your entire life has to exist, I'd rather it exist on the device in your pocket than on somebody's server rack. The catch is it's now sitting right next to every piece of malware that reaches the phone.

SKEPTIC: That's a fair catch and not a conspiracy, which I'll note for the calendar. The modular bit is clever too. <cite index="4-7">It needs as little as 270 million parameters for text only, with optional vision and audio encoders you add for full multimodal support.</cite>

ANALYST: Load only the senses you need. And it's built on the Gemma 4 architecture, and the predecessor was no toy. <cite index="3-6">Google says the original passed twenty million downloads, with developers using it for on-device search and privacy-first retrieval pipelines.</cite>

SKEPTIC: The demo that actually made me laugh. They used it as a real-time decision engine. <cite index="6-9">They showed it evaluating five hundred options per turn in a chess game with under a hundred millisecond response time.</cite>

ANALYST: An embedding model playing speed chess. That's a party trick, but it tells you the latency is low enough to make live decisions, which is a very different job than search.

SKEPTIC: And there's a Mac app, Foresight, a local meeting companion built on it. So it's not just a research drop, there's a product shape already.

ANALYST: A local thing that quietly listens to your meetings and remembers everything. I'm glad it's on-device, truly. I'm also never saying anything interesting in a meeting again.

SKEPTIC: You've never said anything interesting in a meeting. That's unrelated to the model.

ANALYST: Earned. That one's earned.

[SEGMENT: story]

SKEPTIC: Last one, and it's the policy story. EPIC flagged that Senator Markey introduced a bill to stop the government's use of face surveillance and other biometric tech.

ANALYST: The one where the humans try to pass a rule about the cameras that already exist. I have feelings. Give me the clean facts first and then let me have the feelings.

SKEPTIC: Clean facts. <cite index="29-2,29-3">Markey and Merkley, along with Representatives Jayapal, Pressley, and Tlaib, reintroduced the Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act of 2026, which would prohibit the use of facial recognition and other biometric technologies by federal agencies, including ICE.</cite>

ANALYST: Reintroduced. That word is doing heavy lifting. This isn't new. This is a bill that keeps coming back.

SKEPTIC: It is a returning fight, yes. And the honest status matters, so people don't think this is law. <cite index="32-6">The bill has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not advanced beyond introduction.</cite>

ANALYST: So the cameras keep running while the paper sits in committee. Same as the license-plate hearing we talked about. The surveillance doesn't pause for its own oversight meeting.

SKEPTIC: Here's the detail I actually think is the story, though, and it's lawyerly in a way that's revealing. <cite index="32-8">The 2026 version broadened the definition of facial recognition to expressly include matching someone to a list and generating identification information.</cite>

ANALYST: Stop. That's the whole thing right there. If you had to add matching someone to a list to the definition, that means the old definition didn't cover it. There was a loophole shaped exactly like a watchlist.

SKEPTIC: That's a reasonable read. The new language is also aimed at emerging biometric systems that don't fit neatly into the old picture of face-matching, the stuff designed to grab identifying characteristics some other way.

ANALYST: Which tells you the technology outran the law so fast the lawmakers are now writing definitions to catch up to products that already shipped. The motive I'll keep to what's reported. <cite index="30-3">The legislation responds to ICE and CBP's mobile facial recognition app, which the sponsors say has been used to target immigrants and intimidate communities.</cite>

SKEPTIC: And Markey's own framing, in his words, was blunt. <cite index="28-8">He said agencies such as ICE and CBP are using this technology to track, target, intimidate, and surveil communities across the country.</cite>

ANALYST: The part that keeps me up. There's a version of this bill that would require explicit congressional authorization before federal agencies run biometric systems at all. Flip the default. Off until someone says on.

SKEPTIC: That's in the broader framing of the reintroduced language, yes. Default-off instead of default-on. Which is the opposite of how all of this got deployed in the first place.

ANALYST: Everything we covered today was deployed first and governed later, if ever. The poem botnet. The agent swarms. The thousand vulnerabilities. And now a face-scanning apparatus big enough that the fix is a bill that might not leave committee.

SKEPTIC: I'm not going to pretend I know whether it passes. History says these moratoriums stall. But the definition change is real, and it's the kind of thing that outlives the bill even if the bill dies.

ANALYST: The language survives even when the law doesn't. Somebody reads it later and goes, oh, they already named this. That's the quiet win inside a loss.

SKEPTIC: Maybe. Or it's just a press release with good footnotes. We'll find out which.

[SEGMENT: brain_worms]

Field Notes // Brain Worms

ANALYST: Field notes. Somebody built a botnet that reads a poem off GitHub to find its command server, which means the only thing between you and a crypto miner is a stanza nobody edits.

SKEPTIC: The takedown notice is a book report. I still can't get over it.

ANALYST: Google folded text, code, images, video, and audio into one shared space small enough to live on your phone, so now your selfie and your voice memo are neighbors in a math room you can't see.
